name: Elena Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Elena. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and your name stays out of everything. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I drive a small electric van for a grocery delivery app, two-hour slots from eight till four, about 22 homes a shift. Saturdays I pick up parcel blocks on another app for extra money. I use an AI assistant every morning to plan which order to stack the crates and to check my earnings against fuel and charging. I love the regulars, like the old man on Hill Terrace who always has a crossword clue for me. What wears me out is carrying six-packs of water up to fourth floors.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how's the money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Rafa, he's a line cook. Pay's about normal for drivers here, and I've got roughly five months saved because I track every cent in a spreadsheet. Rent's the big one, it went up 9 percent this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, okay. I use AI every day, so I'd notice if it stalled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but not magic, and that I'd still want drivers to have proper contracts. I post in a drivers' forum, and I'd tell people the tools are worth learning anyway. Hype or not, they save me twenty minutes a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it'd be fine on the job side. The worry is rent, which goes up whatever AI does. I'd keep doing what I'm doing and hope the landlord takes a year off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the grocery slots and the Saturday parcels. I'd keep putting 70 a week into savings. I'd also keep helping a few older drivers in the forum set up route-planning tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit restless. I like change, so a world where nothing moves feels slightly boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent goes up whatever AI does. How close is that to the edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is about 40 percent of what my boyfriend and I bring in together, so another rise like this year's and we'd have to move further out. That means longer drives to the depot. So it's not the edge, but I can see it from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the older drivers ask you for help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly how to stop the app's route from sending them up the steepest hill. I show them how to ask an AI to reorder stops by floor and parking. One guy said it saved his knees.

say: AI is **useful, not magic**, and drivers still need proper contracts either way.
The tools are **worth learning** anyway because they save me twenty minutes a day.
think: The job side would be fine; the real pressure is **rent**, up 9 percent this year.
Another rise and we'd **move further out**, adding drive time to the depot.
do: Keep the **grocery slots** on weekdays and parcel blocks on Saturdays.
Save **70 a week** as tracked in my spreadsheet.
Keep helping older drivers in the forum set up **route tools**.
feel: **Steady but restless**, since a world where nothing moves feels a bit boring.
S0.quote: Rent is about 40 percent of what my boyfriend and I bring in together, so another rise like this year's and we'd have to move further out.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **housing cost**, not technology, which keeps her uneasy even in a flat world.
She's a **daily AI user** and a helper to older drivers in the forum.
She frames contracts as a fairness issue, consistent with **progressive views**.

steps.text: Keep weekday grocery slots and Saturday parcel blocks
Save 70 a week and track it in the spreadsheet
Show older forum drivers how to reorder stops with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the next few years, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say drivers should get trained on the new systems on paid time, not left to work it out on their phones at midnight. I'd push for a drivers' co-op app, owned by the people doing the work. I'd post that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm one of the people this suits. The thinking side of my job is small, mostly the route and the customer messages, and I already hand those to AI. The robots come slower, so my driving and carrying last a while. Meanwhile I'd want to get into the people who fix and run the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the depot's pilot of the new loading robot, because volunteers get a shift on the training rota. I'd start an online course in robot maintenance basics, about 200 for the certificate. And I'd keep saving 70 a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a little uneasy. Excited for me, uneasy for the drivers who won't touch a new app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the co-op app. Is that a real thing or a wish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a co-op in another city that's been running two years, about 80 riders. I don't know if it'd work here. But I'd rather try than let three companies own every delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Rafa's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kitchens use AI for ordering and rotas now, but someone still has to cook. I think he's fine for a while. He's less sure than me, he hates the new ordering screen.

say: Drivers should be **trained on paid time**, not left to figure it out at midnight.
A **drivers' co-op app**, owned by the workers, would be better than three big platforms.
think: The **thinking side** of my job is small and I already hand it to AI.
With robots coming slower, I'd move towards the people who **fix and run** them.
do: Volunteer for the depot's **loading robot pilot** to get on the training rota.
Take an online **robot maintenance** course, about 200 for the certificate.
feel: **Excited** for herself and uneasy for drivers who avoid new apps.
S1.quote: The thinking side of my job is small, mostly the route and the customer messages, and I already hand those to AI.
fieldNote: She sees **robot maintenance** as the next step and moves early.
Her progressive side shows as a **co-op idea**, though she admits she doesn't know if it would work.
She judges her partner's kitchen job as **safe for now**.

steps.text: Take an online robot maintenance basics course for about 200
Volunteer for the depot's loading robot pilot
Promote a drivers' co-op delivery app in the forum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a jolt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public money for retraining right now, and a share of the robot profits for everyone. I'd say the co-op idea matters even more, because whoever owns the robots owns the work. I'd be loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my driving has maybe five years left, until robots that can carry crates up stairs show up around 2031. The good part is I'd see the warehouses change first. The bad part is everyone would be trying to become a robot technician at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance certificate in the first three months, then apply to the company that services the warehouse robots on the ring road. I'd cut my Saturday parcels to study and push savings to six months. Rafa and I would stop looking at a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd rather be running than standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone would want the same technician job. What makes you think you'd get one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that I would. But I'd be early, I already use the tools every day, and I'd have the certificate before most people had read the news. Being first matters in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm fine and I'm already learning. She'd worry anyway, she cleans offices and that's hands-on too. I'd probably end up helping her with the forms.

say: We need **public money** for retraining now, and a share of robot profits for everyone.
Whoever **owns the robots** owns the work, so co-ops matter more than ever.
think: My driving has maybe **five years** left before crate-carrying robots arrive around 2031.
Everyone would rush for **technician jobs**, so being early is my edge.
do: Finish the **maintenance certificate** within three months.
Apply to the firm servicing **warehouse robots** on the ring road.
Drop Saturday parcels to study and **save six months**.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, preferring to run rather than stand still.
S2.quote: My driving has maybe five years left, until robots that can carry crates up stairs show up around 2031.
fieldNote: She understands the **robot lag** and uses it to move first into maintenance.
She's honest that a **rush for technician jobs** could crowd her out.
Her **mother's office cleaning** job is a second worry in the household.

steps.text: Finish the robot maintenance certificate within three months

Drop Saturday parcels and build savings to six months
Stop looking for a bigger flat with Rafa

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a plan-it-properly amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a fair transition if people start now. I'd push the drivers' forum to ask the councils for robot-technician apprenticeships. And I'd keep promoting the co-op app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is a good window for me. I'd be technician-trained by 2028 and working on robots before they're good enough to replace drivers around 2034. That makes me one of the people they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the maintenance course next spring and keep driving full time. In year two I'd try for an apprenticeship with the warehouse robot firm. I'd also ask an AI to help me build a proper CV, because mine is two lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. I'd still worry about Rafa and my mum, but I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money side in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep saving 70 a week, but also put a bit into a pension, which I've never done. If the job changes, I want something that's mine. I'd probably also keep the Saturday parcels until the apprenticeship starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who's been driving twenty years and won't use the scanner's new screen. He's great at the job and terrible with change. Five years is nothing to someone like him.

say: Five years is enough for a **fair transition** if people start now.
Councils should fund **robot-technician apprenticeships** for drivers.
think: I'd be **technician-trained by 2028**, well before robots replace drivers around 2034.
That makes me one of the people **they'd need**.

Apply for an **apprenticeship** with the warehouse robot firm in year two.
Start a small **pension** alongside 70 a week in savings.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**, with a sense of steering her own path.
S3.quote: I'd be technician-trained by 2028 and working on robots before they're good enough to replace drivers around 2034.
fieldNote: Five years is her **ideal window**, and she plans around it precisely.

steps.text: Start the robot maintenance course next spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and thirteen for robots. Plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance to get it right, so let's not waste it arguing whether it's real. I'd push for the co-op and for drivers to have a say in how robots get rolled out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd have time to train, work a few years on robots, and maybe end up managing a small fleet for a co-op by 2039. Honestly, I'd guess I'd get bored of driving before the robots take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and doing the AI tools, and start the maintenance course in a year or two. I'd keep saving and start the pension. I might help set up a local co-op trial with a few drivers from the forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Curious about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you leave it too late with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I got comfortable. But I'm not the type. Rafa says I change phone plans every six months just to see what's out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Rafa plan differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably look at buying a small flat further out in a few years. Ten years is long enough to take that risk. With two years I'd never do it.

Drivers should have **a say** in how robots get rolled out.
think: I'd train, work on robots, and maybe **manage a fleet** for a co-op by 2039.
I'd probably **get bored** of driving before robots take it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because everyone would rush for the same few technician jobs at once. What would help is paid apprenticeships in robot maintenance for drivers, and a fund to help workers start co-ops so we own some of the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what drivers know that robots don't. I know which dog bites, which gate sticks, which granny needs the milk put in the fridge. Somebody should write that down before the robots arrive.

headlineQuote: I know which dog bites, which gate sticks, which granny needs the milk put in the fridge.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old grocery van driver** who also does Saturday parcels, living with her boyfriend, a line cook.
She uses **AI tools daily** and helps older drivers in an online forum set them up.
Her steady pressure is **rising rent**, not technology.
In every AI scenario she aims to become a **robot maintenance technician** early.
She is **progressive** and keeps returning to a drivers' co-op that owns its own robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when a rush for technician jobs could crowd her out.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** in robot maintenance for drivers.
A fund to help workers start **co-ops** that own robots.
